text: A node is called good if, on the path from the root down to that node, there is no node with a larger value. Count the good nodes in the tree.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — no larger value on the path means the node's value is greater than or equal to every value above it. So an equal value still counts as good. Is that right?

Good, that greater-or-equal is going to matter later. Two things follow right away. The root is always good, because its path is just itself, so the answer is at least one. And here's what makes this cheap: I don't need the whole path, only one number from it, the maximum. No larger value above me is the same as I'm at least as big as the largest value above me. So the path collapses into a single running max that I carry down.
Are there any constraints on the input size? And what is the value range?
Up to ten to the fifth nodes. Values from negative ten thousand to ten thousand.

A hundred thousand nodes with no promise about shape. One thing worth flagging — the tree could be one long chain, so a recursive solution could be a hundred thousand frames deep. I'll come back to whether that's safe. Let me run through the example: three, one, four, three, null, one, five. The root three is good. Its left child one has max three above it, so not good. That one's child is three, tying the max of three, so good. On the right, four beats three, so good; under it, one is not, and five beats four. That's three, three, four, and five — four good nodes.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to build, for each node, the full path from the root and scan it for a bigger value. That's order of h per node, so n times h — n squared on a chain, about ten billion operations at a hundred thousand. Way too slow. This problem reminds me of a top-down DFS that pushes information down the tree: each call inherits what it needs from its ancestors as a parameter. Here that's just one integer, the max seen so far. So it's a plain preorder DFS with one extra parameter.

Here's the plan. One: an empty node contributes zero. Two: update mx to the max of mx and this node's value, so mx is the largest value on the path including me. Three: count one if my value is at least mx, then add both subtrees, passing the same mx down. One thing worth flagging — I update before I test, which looks backwards. After the update, my value is at least the new max exactly when it's at least the old max, so the two orderings agree — but only because the test is greater-or-equal. With a strict greater-than, updating first makes the test always false, and the answer is zero every time. There's a trade-off here: I could carry the whole path, which generalizes to path follow-ups, but one integer is enough. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's three steps in order: update mx, compare myself with greater-or-equal, and pass the same mx to both children. One thing worth flagging — the INT_MIN sentinel. It's tempting to say it's safe because values only go down to negative ten thousand, but the real reason is the greater-or-equal: even a node holding INT_MIN leaves mx at INT_MIN and still counts. Now, one thing I'm not happy about in my own code: the default argument. goodNodes is the public API, so a caller can write goodNodes of root, five — it compiles, and on the example it silently returns one instead of four. In production I'd make the recursion a private helper, trading a silent bug for a loud one.

Let's dry-run the code on the same example, expecting four. The row that matters is the second three: it sits under one, but the max carried down is still three — the one didn't pull it lower. Three is greater than or equal to three, so it counts. That tie is exactly what greater-or-equal is for; rejecting ties would give three instead of four. The rest is routine, and the total is four. That matches. Corner cases: a null root returns zero at the guard. A single node returns one. A chain going down, five, four, three, two, one, returns one — only the root. And a tree of identical values returns n, since every comparison is a tie.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each node is visited once with constant work. Space is order of h for the recursion stack: about seventeen frames on a balanced tree of a hundred thousand nodes, but a hundred thousand frames on a chain. I measured that rather than guess: without optimization, on the default eight megabyte stack, the crash point is about a hundred thirty thousand frames, so the margin is only about one point three times. Under a one megabyte stack, a hundred-thousand-node chain segfaults. Oh, one more thing — so the honest answer to is this safe is: it depends on the environment. Where I don't control the stack size, I'd rewrite it with an explicit stack of node and max pairs on the heap.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You collapsed the path into a single running max early, then justified the odd update-before-test ordering with a one-line proof — and showed it only works with greater-or-equal. You criticized your own default argument and showed the exact silent wrong answer it allows. And you didn't hand-wave the recursion depth — you reported a thin one point three times margin instead of calling it fine. Good work.
